112-013.r: Mauna Loa (Hawaii, US) → world's largest volcano; erupted in 2022, first time in 38 years. Name means 'Long Mountain'; above-sea part extends about 120 km.

112-014.r: Active volcanoes → Cotopaxi (Ecuador), Etna (Italy), Fujiyama (Japan). Aconcagua (Argentina, near Chile) is a volcanic mountain but not an active volcano.

112-015.r: Active volcanoes → Etna (Sicily, Italy) and Vesuvius (near Naples). Kilimanjaro (Tanzania, Africa's highest peak) is dormant; Aconcagua is non-volcanic.

112-017.r: Kilimanjaro → volcano in north-eastern Tanzania, Africa's highest mountain; three cones Kibo, Mawenzi, Shira; top is Uhuru peak on Kibo (earlier Kaiser-Wilhelm-Spitze).

112-018.r: 'Lighthouse of the Mediterranean' → Stromboli, on Stromboli island north of Sicily (Italy); its continuous gaseous eruptions light up the area.

112-019.r: Arctic region → near the North Pole; Antarctica (fifth largest continent, fully ice-covered) → contains the South Pole. Also asked: Stromboli is an active volcano.

112-021.r: Most active volcano → Kilauea (Hawaii Island, USA); next Etna (Italy), then Piton de la Fournaise and Nyamuragira.

112-022.r: Etna → Sicily; Vesuvius → Italy (Bay of Naples); Erebus → Ross Island (Antarctica); Cotopaxi → Ecuador (Andes).

112-023.r: Mount Rainier → U.S.A.; Etna → Italy; Paricutin → Mexico; Taal → Philippines.

112-024.r: Mount Kinabalu → Malaysia; Elburz → Iran; Aconcagua → Argentina; Kilimanjaro → Tanzania.

112-025.r: Sabancaya → Peru; Mount Etna → Italy; Colima → Mexico; Merapi → Indonesia.

112-026.r: Indonesia (book's figures) → more than 17,000 islands; about 150 volcanoes in total, of which about 80 are active.
112-026.c: The book prints (b) Only 2, but its own figures (over 17,000 islands; about 80 active volcanoes) make statement 1 true and statement 2 false.

112-027.r: Karakatoa (Krakatau) volcano → in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra, Indonesia.

112-028.r: Mount Rainier → U.S.A.; Mount Etna → Italy; Mount Paricutin → Mexico; Mount Apo → Philippines.

113-001.r: Plate tectonics → developed in the late 1960s by many (Wilson, Morgan, Parker, McKenzie, Harry Hess), so 'given by H.H. Hess in 1967' is false; it rests on sea-floor spreading.

113-002.r: Earthquake waves → P (primary, fastest) and S (secondary), both body waves, plus L (surface waves: Love and Rayleigh). So 'P.S.L.'

113-003.r: Each earthquake has its own, different shadow zone (I true). II false: beyond 105° P waves have a shadow band and S waves are stopped by the liquid outer core.

113-004.r: 'Ring of Fire' → Pacific Ocean belt of volcanoes and earthquakes (about 90% of world's earthquakes): Chile, California, Alaska, Japan, Philippines, New Zealand. Not forest fires.

113-005.r: Richter scale (Charles Richter, 1935) → logarithmic, base 10: +1 magnitude = 10 times amplitude and 32 times energy, not 100. Only statement 1 true.

113-006.r: Intensity → Mercalli scale; magnitude → energy released, depends on wave amplitude. Each Richter step = 32 times energy, not 100. Statements 1, 2, 3 true.
113-006.t: Mercalli scale measures intensity; Richter scale measures magnitude.

113-007.r: Richter scale → measures earthquakes; strictly it gives magnitude, while intensity is on the Mercalli scale. The book accepts 'intensity of earthquake' as the closest option.

113-009.r: Seismometer → records earthquakes; crescograph → growth of plants; cardiogram → heartbeat.

113-010.r: Seismograph → instrument that detects and records seismic waves; seismometer is its sensing part (often a synonym); seismogram is the recording made.

113-011.r: 'Tsunami' → Japanese word: 'tsu' = harbour, 'nami' = wave ('harbour wave'); high waves caused by earthquakes.

113-012.r: Wrong statement → 'killed more than 50 lakh'. The 26 December 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami (off Sumatra, Indonesia) killed about 2-3 lakh people.

113-013.r: Fukushima (Japan) → 11 March 2011 earthquake (magnitude 9.0) and tsunami damaged nuclear power plants, leaking radiation.

113-014.r: North-West Indian subcontinent is earthquake-prone → plate tectonic activity: convergence of the Indian and Eurasian plates.

113-015.r: Epicentre → place on the surface where seismic waves are first recorded; focus → point inside the Earth where energy is released.
113-015.t: Focus is the underground origin; epicentre is the surface point above it.

113-016.r: Cocos Plate → lies between Central America and the Pacific Plate.

114-001.r: Most countries → Africa (54); then Europe 49, Asia 48, North America 23, Oceania 14, South America 12.

114-003.r: Largest continent → Asia (44,568,500 sq km); among the options, Africa (30,065,000). Order: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, Australia.

114-004.r: Guyana → South America (capital George Town), not Africa; Gabon, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau are African. Area order: Africa > South America > Europe > Australia.
114-004.t: Don't confuse Guyana (South America) with Guinea or Guinea-Bissau (West Africa).

114-006.r: Continents by area (descending): Asia, Africa, North America, … Europe, Australia. Smallest → Australia; two smallest → Australia and Europe.

114-009.r: Share of Earth's land (Philip's Atlas): Asia 29.8%, Africa 20.3%, North America 16.2%, South America 11.8%, Antarctica 9.2%, Europe 6.8%, Australia 5.9%.

114-010.r: Maximum per capita land → Australia (World Bank data).

114-011.r: Highest mean elevation → Antarctica (about 2300 m); Asia 923 m, North America 760 m, Africa 585 m, South America 554 m, Australia 330 m, Europe 302 m.

114-012.r: South America map: 1 → Andes, 2 → Brazilian Shield, 3 → Guiana Highland, 4 → Amazon Basin.

114-013.r: Correct pair → Atlas Mountains: North-Western Africa. Abyssinian Plateau → East Africa; Guiana Highlands → northern South America; Okavango Basin → South-Western Africa.

114-014.r: Highest percentage of plains in total area → Europe (South America also has large plains).

114-015.r: Aconcagua → South America; Meseta → Europe; Serengeti Plains → Africa; Gibson Desert → Australia.

114-016.r: Guyana → northern South America (only South American nation with English as official language), not Africa. Gabon (Libreville), Guinea (Conakry), Guinea-Bissau (Bissau) are African.

114-017.r: Not Australian → Salween (Salvin) Valley, in the Arunachal Pradesh region of India. Australian: Lake Eyre basin (largest internal drainage), Nullarbor Plain (south coast), Mount Selwyn.

115-001.r: West to East: Pontic (Turkiye, south of the Black Sea) → Zagros (Iran) → Hindu Kush → Karakoram. From the Pamir knot, Hindu Kush runs west, Karakoram east.

115-002.r: Darling Range → South-Western coast of Australia (Western Australia).

115-003.r: 'Sea of Mountains' → British Columbia; name from Molyneux St. John's book on Lord Dufferin's 1876 tour through British Columbia.

115-004.r: World's highest peaks (e.g. Mount Everest in the Himalayas) → mostly in young folded mountains.

115-005.r: Longest mountain range → Andes (7000–8900 km, along South America's west coast); Rockies over 4800 km; Himalayas about 2500 km.

115-006.r: Oldest mountains of South America → Pacaraima (Guiana Highlands): tepui plateaus about 1.8 billion years old (Precambrian), crystalline block mountains.

115-007.r: Not a young folded mountain → Sierra Nevada (block mountain, California, USA); Rocky, Himalaya, Alps are young folded. Andes → South America.

115-010.r: Longest range → Andes (7000–8900 km); Rocky 4800 km; Himalaya 2500 km; Alps 1200 km (Europe's longest).

115-011.r: Longest surface mountain range → Andes, on South America's west (Pacific) coast. Of Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Paraguay, Venezuela, it crosses only four.

115-013.r: Andes → along the entire west coast of South America, through seven countries: Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina.
115-013.h: 'Very Cold Evenings Push Brave Climbers Away' = Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina.

115-014.r: Southern Alps → South Island of New Zealand (west side); highest peak Aoraki/Mount Cook, 3724 m.

115-015.r: Lengths (book's data): Andes 7000–8900 km > Rocky 4800 > Great Dividing Range 3700 > Himalaya 2500. Book takes (b) Andes, Rocky, Himalaya, Great Dividing as nearest.
115-015.c: The book prints (b) only as the 'nearest' option; its own figures put the Great Dividing Range (3700 km) ahead of the Himalaya (2500 km).

115-016.r: Alps → France, Austria, Germany, Switzerland, just north of the Mediterranean; not England. Highest peak Mont Blanc (4,807 m); young folded mountains.

115-018.r: Andes → South America; Altai → Asia; Alps → Europe; Appalachian → North America.

115-019.r: White Mountains → New Hampshire and Maine states, U.S.A.

115-020.r: India–Myanmar boundary → Arakan Yoma range (Himalayan extension in western Myanmar; hills Naga, Chin, Lushai, Patkoi). Khasi Hills (Meghalaya) are not on it, so 'None of the above'.

115-022.r: Black Forest → block mountain in Germany; the Vosges (France) are another block mountain.

115-023.r: Black Forest → mountain range in Germany; highest peak Feldberg (1493 m).

115-024.r: Along the Rhine → Black Forest on its east, Vosges on its west. Rhine rises in the Swiss Alps, flows to the North Sea; Bonn and Cologne lie on it.

115-025.r: Black Mountains → North Carolina, U.S.A.; part of the Appalachian Mountains.

115-026.r: Odd one out → Appalachian: old mountains of the Caledonian period. Alps, Andes, Himalayas (also Rocky, Atlas) are Tertiary (Alpine) folded mountains.

115-028.r: Not old folded → Andes (young folded, like Rocky, Alps, Himalaya). Ural, Aravalli and Appalachian are old folded mountains.

115-029.r: Correct rows: Appalachians (North America) fold; Andes (South America) fold. Wrong: Vosges are block mountains of Europe; Alps are fold mountains. Only two correct.

115-030.r: Pennines (Europe), Appalachians (North America), Aravallis (India) → old mountains: stopped growing once plate movement stopped.

115-031.r: Drakensberg → range mainly in South Africa and Lesotho; highest peak Thabana Ntlenyana (3482 m, Lesotho).

115-032.r: Atlas Mountains → Africa (across Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia).

115-033.r: Atlas Mountains (Africa) → about 2400 km through Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia; five ranges separating Mediterranean climate from the Sahara.

115-034.r: Allegheny → U.S.A.; Cantabrian → Spain; Elburz → Iran; Mackenzie → Canada.

115-035.r: Kosciuszko (2228 m) → Australia; McKinley (6190 m) → North America; Elbrus (5642 m) → Europe, not Asia; Kilimanjaro (5895 m) → Africa.

115-037.r: Kilimanjaro → Tanzania; Toubkal → Morocco; Stanley → Uganda; Hoggar → Algeria.

115-038.r: Alps → folded mountain; Vosges → block mountain; Vindhya → residual mountain; Fujiyama → volcanic mountain.

115-039.r: Mount Titlis → Switzerland (Black Forest → Germany; Rocky → North America).

115-040.r: Apennine → Italy (about 1350 km; highest peak Corno Grande, 2914 m). Pyrenees → France–Spain; Jura → France–Switzerland; Dinaric Alps → Balkan countries.

115-041.r: Spain–France boundary → Pyrenees, from the Bay of Biscay to the Mediterranean Sea.

115-042.r: Spain–France → Pyrenees; Switzerland → Alps (highest Mont Blanc, about 4807 m); Bulgaria → Balkan; Italy → Apennine.

115-045.r: Golan Heights → Middle East: a rocky plateau in south-west Syria, occupied by Israel in the 1967 war.

115-046.r: Basic landform → volcanic cone (ejecta, lava and ash piled around a vent, with a central crater); residual mountain, monadnock, erosional waterfall come from erosion.

115-047.r: Elbrus → Russia (Europe's highest, 5642 m); Kilimanjaro → Tanzania (5895 m); Mt. Cook → New Zealand (3,724 m); McKinley (Denali) → U.S.A. (6190 m).

115-048.r: Atlas → Morocco; Kilimanjaro → Tanzania; Chimborazo → Ecuador; Pyrenees → France/Spain.

115-049.r: Taurus Mountains → along the Mediterranean coast of Asia Minor (Turkey); southern boundary of the Anatolian plateau.

115-050.r: Epeirogenic forces (endogenic) → vertical earth movements: uplift/emergence and subsidence/sinking of large parts of the crust.
115-050.t: Don't confuse with orogenic forces, which build mountains by folding.

116-001.r: Tibetan (Qinghai-Tibetan) Plateau → average elevation over 4500 m (nearest option 5 km); area about 2.5 million sq km.

116-002.r: 'Storehouse of minerals' in South America → Patagonia Plateau (book's answer).

116-003.r: City on a plateau → Madrid (Meseta Plateau, 610–760 m). Bucharest 55.8 m, Jamnagar 20 m, Singapore 15 m above sea level.

116-004.r: 'Roof of the World' → Pamir Plateau: very high, meeting point of many mountains, southern border of Central Asia.

116-005.r: Largest plateau of the options → Colorado (150580 sq miles); Columbia 105633, Coconino 5000, Aquarius 900. World's largest → Tibetan Plateau.

116-006.r: Telegraphic Plateau → part of the North Atlantic Ridge, between Newfoundland and Ireland.

116-007.r: Wrong pair → Telegraph Plateau – Indian Ocean (it is in the Atlantic). Correct: Cocoa Ridge – Pacific; Walvis Ridge – Atlantic; Agulhas Basin – Indian Ocean.

117-001.r: Death Valley (California, USA) → a rift valley: linear lowland formed by a geological rift or fault.

117-002.r: 'Devil's Golf Course' → large salt pan on the floor of Death Valley (Death Valley National Park, northern Mojave Desert), mainly California, U.S.A.

117-003.r: Death Valley (California, USA) → known for excessive heat: hottest and most arid valley of the USA; lowest place in North America (–86 m).

117-005.r: Panjshir Valley → north-eastern Afghanistan, about 150 km north of Kabul near the Hindu Kush; a main battleground of the Soviet war.

117-006.r: Silicon Valley → southern San Francisco Bay area, California, U.S.A.; famous for making computer chips.

117-007.r: Taylor Valley → Antarctica; discovered by Robert Falcon Scott in 1903, who named it 'Valley of the Dead'.

117-008.r: Great Artesian Basin → Australia; one of the world's largest underground water reservoirs (about 1.7 million sq km), west of the Great Dividing Range.

117-009.r: Great Basin → U.S.A., between the Rocky Mountains and Sierra Nevada; Columbia Plateau to the north, Mojave and Sonoran deserts to the south.

117-010.r: Valley of the Kings (Wadi-el Muluk) → Egypt.

117-011.r: Blind (steephead) valley → deep, narrow, flat-bottomed valley ending abruptly; found in limestone (Karst) regions.

117-012.r: Hanging valley → glacial erosion: a tributary glacier's valley is left higher than the main valley, often with a waterfall (e.g. Yosemite Valley, USA).

117-013.r: Karst landform → sinkhole (doline): a closed depression, the most common landform in karst (limestone) areas.

118-001.r: Most hot deserts → western margins of continents, 15º–30º N and S (Sahara, Kalahari, Atacama), as trade winds turn dry moving west. A and R true, R explains A.

118-002.r: Deserts → source of perennial energy: in six hours they get more solar energy than mankind uses in a year (Gerhard Knies). A and R true, R explains A.

118-003.r: Desert → area with annual rainfall less than 25 cm.

118-004.r: Deserts most likely near the tropics (option 'twenty-three degrees latitude'): high pressure with descending winds, dry trade winds on west coasts, rain shadows, continental interiors.

118-005.r: Interior Australia is desert/semi-desert (about 70 percent arid or semi-arid): A true. Northern Australia is tropical, not temperate (south is temperate): R false.

118-006.r: Least desertification → Europe, the only continent without a desert. Desertification (UNCCD) = land degradation in drylands from climate and human activities.

118-007.r: Biggest (non-polar) desert → Sahara, North Africa (about 3.6 million square miles).

118-009.r: Most densely populated desert → Thar (83 people per sq km).

118-010.r: Takla Makan desert → south-western Xinjiang, north-west China.

118-011.r: Wrong pair → Gibson – Brazil: Gibson Desert is in Western Australia. Correct: Sonoran – USA; Taklamakan – China; Karakum – Turkmenistan.

118-012.r: Kara Kum (Kara-Kum) desert → mainly Turkmenistan, with some part in Kazakhstan; the book accepts both.

118-013.r: Dasht-e-Lut → large salt desert in Iran (Kerman, Sistan and Baluchestan); world's warmest desert per NASA's Aqua satellite (2005).

118-014.r: Gobi Desert → southern Mongolia and northern China; surrounded by the Alashan, Tienshan and Altai mountains.

118-015.r: Gobi (cold desert of Asia) → only Mongolia and China; does not reach Russia or Kazakhstan. Altai Mountains lie to its north-west.

118-016.r: Smallest to largest: Great Sandy (Australia, 284,993 sq km) < Gobi (1,300,000) < Arabian (2,300,000; second largest) < Sahara (8,600,000 sq km).

118-017.r: Largest desert of South Asia → Thar ('Great Indian Desert', NW India–SE Pakistan). Atacama → Chile, Peru; Colorado → USA, Mexico; Kalahari → Botswana, Namibia, South Africa.

118-018.r: Atacama (South America) → driest place on Earth; rich in sodium nitrate and copper; lies in northern Chile and southern Peru, not southern Chile.
118-018.t: Atacama is in northern Chile, not southern Chile.

118-021.r: Temperate desert → Patagonian Desert; other temperate deserts: Gobi and Ladakh. Arabian, Atacama and Kalahari are not.

118-022.r: Tropical deserts → trade wind belt on western sides of continents (1 true). Eastern Himalaya gets more rain from southwest winds of the Bay of Bengal, not north-east (2 false).

118-023.r: Kalahari Desert (930000 sq km, interior Southern Africa) → mainly Botswana, parts of Namibia and South Africa.

118-024.r: Southern Hemisphere desert → Kalahari (Botswana, Namibia, South Africa); name from Tswana 'Kgala' = 'the great thirst'.

118-025.r: African–Eurasian desert belt → sub-tropical high-pressure cells (1 true); warm ocean currents are not a necessary cause, e.g. the Gobi (2 false).

118-026.r: Desert-dwelling animals → xerocoles. Fossorial → digging/underground; arboreal → in trees; terrestrial → on land.

118-027.r: Great Victoria Desert → Western Australia and South Australia; Australia's largest desert (348,750 sq km).

118-028.r: Gobi → Asia; Patagonia → South America; Victoria → Australia; Kalahari → Southern Africa.

119-001.r: Steppes → Russia; Prairies → U.S.A.; Velds (Welds) → South Africa; Downs → Australia. Tropical grasslands: Savanna (Africa), Llanos (Venezuela, Colombia), Campos (Brazil).

119-002.r: Wrong pair → Veld – Australia (Veld is in South Africa). Correct: Prairies – North America; Pampas – South America; Steppes – Europe.

119-003.r: Llanos → South America; Steppe → Europe; Prairies → North America; Veld → Africa.

119-004.r: Correct pair → Argentina – Pampas (also Uruguay, Brazil). Campos → Brazilian Highland; Savanna → East Africa (Kenya, Tanzania); Steppes → Eastern Europe, Central Asia.

119-005.r: Savanna (grassland with shrubs, scattered trees, between rainforest and desert) → most widespread in East Africa; also Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela, southern India.

119-006.r: Mid-latitude grassland of South America → Pampas (Argentina, Uruguay, southern Brazil). Others: Prairie (North America), Downs (Australia).
